newsitem.title: PERU: Peru pension funds seen doubling in size by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Peru pension funds seen doubling in size by 2000.

text.p: Four years after their creation, Peru's private pension funds have consolidated an important role in the national savings structure and are set to double in size over the next three years, industry officials said.

Since their creation in 1993, Peru's Administrators of Pension Funds (AFP) have accumulated over $1.4 billion through 1,659,179 contrbutors and are expected to grow to over 1.8 million members by the end of the year.
"In this country, AFPs are a reality," said AFP President Jaime Caceres. "By the year 2000 the funds will double to $3 billion."
AFP superintendent Augusto Mouchard said the private funds had had to overcome the popular suspicion of pension funds associated with the previous state system.
"The problems that had confronted the (previous) national pension systems prevented them from fulfilling their duties to the pensioners," said Mouchard.

AFP executives added that the private funds have acted as a lever to the development of the country by injecting capital into the economy, which in turn fortified the banking system and attracted more investors.
"The private pensions system is important for the economic stability of the country," said the financial manager for AFP Integra, Jorge Ramos.
Integra, the largest of Peru's five AFPs with 30 percent of the pension funds, is expecting to increase its investment portfolio to $600 million. Last year investors brought in $370 million.
Over the past 12 months, AFP funds have grown 25.17 percent nominally and 15.06 percent in real terms. Inflation during the same time period was 9.48 percent, the lowest in 25 years.
"The success of the pension funds is demonstrated by the good performance of the Lima Stock Exchange," said Ramos. The Lima bolsa rose more than 50 percent over the first half of 1997.

AFPs have grown at an average annual rate of 23.20 percent nominally and 9.2 percent in real terms since their birth in 1993, and experts predict long term profitability to be between seven and nine percent.
The Peruvian AFP is based on the highly successful Chilean model, now being adopted in Argentina, Uruguay, Mexico, Venezuela and Central America.
Chile, which was the first country to introduce a private pension plan in Latin America 16 years ago, currently holds over $30 billion in pension assets.
The five AFPs in Peru can currently invest in government security bonds, stocks on the Lima bolsa, company bonds and bank deposits.

Recently, the Peruvian Central Bank allowed AFPs to invest up to five percent of their funds in Brady bonds and established investment limits for nine other instruments such as company securities, real estate and mutual funds.
Ramos was critical of the government for its slowness in allowing AFPs to invest in the Brady bonds market.
"We had negotiated for over half a year, and now we will be able to use this instrument," he said. "But the prices have risen and we are at a disadvantage from other investors."
